title: The Hotter the Pan, the Longer Water Survives

scenes.text: Water on a scorching pan should vanish in a flash. Instead, it skates around like it's alive.
label: LEIDENFROST EFFECT
Water on a very hot pan

hud.label: Pan temperature
hud.sub: at or above the Leidenfrost point

scenes.text: Normally, a drop touching hot metal boils fast. Heat pours in, steam escapes, and the drop is gone.
But keep heating, and something flips. Past a certain temperature, a hotter pan makes the drop last longer.

scenes.question: What is holding this drop up?
scenes.heading: A DROP ON A HOT PLATE
scenes.text: Look at the gap. The bottom of the drop flash-boils and creates a thin layer of vapour, a fraction of a millimetre thick. The drop floats on its own steam. And steam conducts heat badly, so the drop barely heats up and lasts far longer.

scenes.heading: DROP LIFETIME vs PAN HEAT
scenes.text: Below roughly two hundred degrees, the drop touches and boils fast. Above it, the cushion forms, and the lifetime shoots up.

scenes.label: JOHANN GOTTLOB LEIDENFROST, 1756
scenes.text: The effect carries the name of Johann Gottlob Leidenfrost, who described it in 1756.
Then, in 2015, UK physicists swapped water for a block of dry ice, frozen carbon dioxide.
Dry ice never melts on hot metal. It sublimes, and rides on its own gas.
label: NATURE COMMUNICATIONS, 2015
Wells et al., lab footage

scenes.text: Cut ratchet teeth into the metal, and the escaping gas pushes the ice. It drives a rotor.
label: A HEAT ENGINE RUNNING ON ICE
Sublimation heat engine
scenes.fact: THE GAS CUSHION CAN PUSH,\NNOT JUST LIFT

scenes.text: Now drop a very hot metal ball in water. It wraps itself in vapour, until the film collapses.
label: HOT METAL IN WATER
Vapour film, then collapse

scenes.text: Liquid nitrogen, at minus 196 degrees, does the same on a room-temperature desk.
label: LIQUID NITROGEN
Boils at about -196 °C

scenes.text: So when water dances on your pan, it's riding on its own steam. If even a solid can do it, what else could we make float? Subscribe, and watch the next one.

shorts.title: Water That Floats on a Hot Pan

scenes.text: This pan is far above one hundred degrees, yet the water lingers instead of flashing away.
It's the Leidenfrost effect. Past roughly two hundred degrees, a drop floats on its own vapour.
That steam cushion insulates the drop, so a hotter pan makes it last longer. The full story is on the channel — subscribe for the next one.

shorts.title: Liquid That Skates on the Floor

scenes.text: Liquid nitrogen is minus one hundred ninety-six degrees. Poured out, it skates instead of splashing.
Dry ice does the same trick. It turns straight from solid to gas, and floats on that gas.
In 2015, UK scientists used that gas cushion to spin a turbine. The full story is on the channel — subscribe for the next one.

youtube.title: The Hotter the Pan, the Longer Water Survives
youtube.description:
Hotter pan, longer life: water can float on its own steam, and a block of dry ice can spin a turbine. Here is the Leidenfrost effect, and the lab experiment that turned it into an engine.

In this video:
- Why a drop of water lasts longer on a hotter pan
- The vapour cushion under the drop
- The 2015 dry ice "sublimation heat engine"
- A hot ball in water, and liquid nitrogen on a desk
